practice_items.atom_title: Adversary skill levels (low-skilled vs high-skilled / zero-days); motivation
practice_items.prompt: An attacker at a coffee shop runs a freely downloaded packet-capture script without understanding how it works. Which tier best describes this adversary?
options: High-skilled
Nation-state
Low-skilled
Zero-day operator
practice_items.explain: Using off-the-shelf tools without understanding the mechanics is the defining characteristic of a low-skilled adversary (script kiddie).

practice_items.atom_title: Adversary skill levels (low-skilled vs high-skilled / zero-days); motivation
practice_items.prompt: A zero-day vulnerability is dangerous primarily because:
options: It only works on Windows systems
It requires a physical connection to exploit
It can only be used by government agencies
The vendor has not yet released a patch, so defenders have no fix available
practice_items.explain: Zero-day means zero days of vendor warning, no patch exists, leaving all users of the affected software exposed.

practice_items.atom_title: Adversary skill levels (low-skilled vs high-skilled / zero-days); motivation
practice_items.prompt: Which of the following motivations would lead an attacker to target a SPECIFIC high-value individual rather than sweeping widely? (Select ALL that apply.)
options: Financial gain (bulk credential resale)
Espionage (stealing trade secrets)
Curiosity / learning
Targeted corporate sabotage
practice_items.explain: Espionage and targeted sabotage require a specific victim. Bulk credential resale and curiosity are typically opportunistic and sweep broadly.

practice_items.atom_title: Adversary skill levels (low-skilled vs high-skilled / zero-days); motivation
practice_items.prompt: Name ONE observable behavior that would place an attacker firmly in the high-skilled tier.
practice_items.explain: High-skill markers include zero-day exploitation, custom tool development, and the ability to adapt when initial attacks fail.

practice_items.atom_title: Adversary skill levels (low-skilled vs high-skilled / zero-days); motivation
practice_items.prompt: Why does the skill tier of an adversary matter for a risk assessment?
options: Higher skill means the attacker is always caught faster
Skill tier determines the breadth and precision of possible attacks, shaping both likelihood and severity
Low-skilled attackers always cause more damage
Skill tier has no effect on the attacks they can perform
practice_items.explain: Low-skilled attacks are broad but shallow; high-skilled attacks are precise and deep. Skill tier directly changes both how many victims are reachable and how severe the harm can be.

practice_items.atom_title: Evil twin attack
practice_items.prompt: What does BSSID stand for and why is it relevant to detecting an evil twin?
options: Broadband Service Signal ID, it tells you the ISP providing the connection
Basic Security Standard ID, it encodes the encryption type in use
Broadcast SSID, it is the human-readable name the user sees in the network list
Basic Service Set Identifier, it is the hardware MAC address of the AP radio, unique per physical device
practice_items.explain: BSSID is the MAC address of the physical radio broadcasting the network. Two APs cannot share the same BSSID legitimately; an evil twin will have a different BSSID from the real AP even if the SSID matches.

practice_items.atom_title: Evil twin attack
practice_items.prompt: A wireless scan shows two entries: both broadcast SSID 'AirportFree', one with security WPA2 and one with OPEN. Select ALL indicators that suggest an evil twin is present.
options: The same SSID is advertised by more than one BSSID
One entry has weaker (or no) security than the other for the same SSID
Both entries have the same signal strength
The network name contains the word 'Free'
practice_items.explain: Duplicate SSID across multiple BSSIDs is a primary evil-twin indicator. A security downgrade (WPA2 vs. OPEN) for the same SSID is a secondary indicator. Signal strength and network name alone are not definitive.

practice_items.atom_title: Evil twin attack
practice_items.prompt: Which attack does an evil twin primarily enable once the victim connects?
options: SQL injection against the victim's database
Man-in-the-middle, the attacker relays and can read or alter all victim traffic
Distributed denial-of-service against a remote server
Brute-force of the victim's Wi-Fi password
practice_items.explain: Once connected to the evil twin, all victim traffic flows through the attacker's hardware, enabling a man-in-the-middle position.

practice_items.atom_title: Evil twin attack
practice_items.prompt: An enterprise legitimately deploys three access points all broadcasting SSID 'CorpNet' with three different BSSIDs. A fourth entry appears with SSID 'CorpNet' and a BSSID not on the approved list. What does this indicate?
options: Normal, any AP can join a corporate SSID
The network is using WPA3, which always shows extra BSSIDs
A misconfigured legitimate AP that should be rebooted
A potential evil twin; the unknown BSSID is not an approved radio
practice_items.explain: An unapproved BSSID broadcasting an authorized SSID is the classic WIDS alert for an evil twin. Multiple BSSIDs per SSID are normal in enterprise deployments, but each BSSID must be on the approved list.

practice_items.atom_title: Evil twin attack
practice_items.prompt: Name two defenses an END USER (not an administrator) can use to reduce evil-twin risk.
practice_items.explain: End-user defenses include: using a VPN to encrypt all traffic regardless of the network, always checking for HTTPS, disabling auto-connect to open networks, and confirming the correct SSID with venue staff before connecting.

practice_items.atom_title: Jamming / denial-of-service attack
practice_items.prompt: Which Wi-Fi access mechanism does RF jamming exploit to deny service?
options: WPA3 handshake, jamming corrupts the 4-way handshake
CSMA/CA, devices back off when they detect channel noise, including deliberate jamming
DHCP, jamming prevents IP address assignment
DNS, jamming reroutes domain lookups
practice_items.explain: Wi-Fi uses CSMA/CA: devices listen before transmitting and back off when they detect noise. A jammer floods the channel with noise, causing all devices to wait indefinitely.

practice_items.atom_title: Jamming / denial-of-service attack
practice_items.prompt: What distinguishes RF jamming from ordinary transient interference (e.g. a nearby microwave)?
options: Jamming always operates on 5 GHz; microwaves only affect 2.4 GHz
Only jamming uses radio waves; interference uses wired signals
Jamming raises RSSI; interference lowers it
Jamming produces sustained, high-level noise across many consecutive samples; interference is typically brief
practice_items.explain: The detection key is duration: a jammer maintains elevated noise over many consecutive readings, while household interference (microwave, Bluetooth) causes momentary spikes.

practice_items.atom_title: Jamming / denial-of-service attack
practice_items.prompt: Select ALL defenses that can help a network survive or detect a jamming attack.
options: Switch to a different Wi-Fi channel not targeted by the jammer
Enable WPA3 encryption
Deploy a WIDS configured to alert on sustained noise-floor anomalies
Move from 2.4 GHz to 5 GHz or 6 GHz to use channels with shorter jammer range
practice_items.explain: Channel switching and frequency-band migration reduce exposure to a narrow-band jammer. A WIDS can detect sustained noise anomalies. WPA3 encrypts data but provides no protection against RF jamming, which operates at the physical layer below encryption.

practice_items.atom_title: Jamming / denial-of-service attack
practice_items.prompt: In the coding problem, solve(samples) returns True when noise samples indicate jamming. Which rule does it apply?
options: Any single sample exceeds the threshold
The average of all samples exceeds the threshold
More than half the samples exceed the threshold
At least N consecutive samples all exceed threshold T
practice_items.explain: The consecutive-sample rule (N or more samples in a row above T) detects sustained interference while ignoring brief transient spikes.

practice_items.atom_title: Jamming / denial-of-service attack
practice_items.prompt: Name the metric, always a negative number, that wireless monitors use to measure signal power.
practice_items.explain: RSSI (Received Signal Strength Indicator), measured in dBm (always negative for Wi-Fi; e.g. -55 dBm).

practice_items.atom_title: War driving; protecting yourself (verify SSIDs, avoid open networks, VPN)
practice_items.prompt: What does a war driver primarily collect about nearby Wi-Fi networks?
options: User passwords transmitted over the networks
SSIDs, BSSIDs, security types, signal strengths, and GPS locations
The names of devices connected to each network
The browsing history of users on each network
practice_items.explain: War driving collects network-level metadata: SSID (name), BSSID (hardware address), security protocol, signal strength, and location. Passwords and browsing history require active attacks beyond passive scanning.

practice_items.atom_title: War driving; protecting yourself (verify SSIDs, avoid open networks, VPN)
practice_items.prompt: Select ALL factors that a personal risk-assessment protocol should check before connecting to a public Wi-Fi network.
options: Whether the SSID has been verified with venue staff
Whether the network is open (no password)
The brand of the router hardware
Whether you have an active VPN
practice_items.explain: The three-step protocol: (1) verify the SSID, (2) avoid open networks, (3) use a VPN. Router brand is not a user-accessible or reliable risk indicator.

practice_items.atom_title: War driving; protecting yourself (verify SSIDs, avoid open networks, VPN)
practice_items.prompt: Why does SSID verification come FIRST in the personal Wi-Fi safety protocol, before VPN activation?
options: VPNs are slower than SSID checks
Venue staff can configure the VPN for you
Connecting to the wrong network (evil twin) sends traffic to an adversary before the VPN tunnel is established
Open networks cannot run VPN software
practice_items.explain: If you connect to a rogue network first, even a brief unencrypted window before the VPN activates can leak credentials. Verification prevents the initial connection from being adversarial.

practice_items.atom_title: War driving; protecting yourself (verify SSIDs, avoid open networks, VPN)
practice_items.prompt: An attacker uses a public war-driving database to learn a corporation's SSID, then includes it in a phishing email. Which attack combination does this illustrate?
options: SQL injection combined with brute-force
Physical-layer reconnaissance combined with social engineering
Jamming combined with man-in-the-middle
Port scanning combined with evil twin
practice_items.explain: War driving provides physical-layer intelligence (SSID) that increases the plausibility of a social-engineering attack, illustrating how passive reconnaissance feeds active attacks.

practice_items.atom_title: War driving; protecting yourself (verify SSIDs, avoid open networks, VPN)
practice_items.prompt: Name the one protection that defends you against interception even if the public Wi-Fi network is legitimate but compromised.
practice_items.explain: A VPN encrypts traffic before it leaves your device, so even a compromised or malicious access point sees only ciphertext.
